The Big lutrine opossum (Lutreolina crassicaudata) is a semiaquatic didelphid that occupies riparian habitats across much of South America. Neonates are remarkably altricial, weighing a mere 0.1 grams [Wwb = 0.1 grams] at birth, a mass that underscores the extremely abbreviated gestation period typical of marsupials. The gestation period itself lasts only 14 days [tg = 14 days] under the typical maternal body temperature of 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C], aligning with the rapid foetal development strategies seen across the Didelphidae. This brief intrauterine phase is followed by an extended period of postnatal development within the pouch, during which the offspring are continuously attached to a teat and undergo most organogenesis. The timing of weaning, when pups become nutritionally independent from milk, occurs at 84 days after birth [tx = 84 days after birth] at 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C], a milestone that reflects the relatively prolonged lactation period in this species compared to smaller didelphids. Juveniles at this stage have attained a wet weight of approximately 95 grams [Wwx = approximately 95 grams], a body size that positions them for independent foraging in dense aquatic vegetation.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a characteristic feature of many lutrine mammals. Females reach an ultimate wet weight of 500 grams [Wwi = 500 grams], while males achieve a substantially larger asymptotic mass of 1200 grams [Wwi = 1200 grams]. This nearly 2.5-fold difference in adult size is among the most extreme documented within the Didelphidae, likely driven by intrasexual selection for male competitive ability during seasonal breeding aggregations. The larger body size in males may also confer advantages in defending access to riparian territories with abundant prey resources. Such marked dimorphism has implications for the species' energetic ecology, influencing daily food intake, metabolic expenditure, and space use patterns. Field studies have shown that adult males maintain larger home ranges than females, a pattern that correlates with their greater energetic demands. The observed dimorphism also shapes the timing of key life-history events, as females must allocate substantial resources to both somatic growth and reproductive effort during their comparatively shorter lives, a constraint that is less pronounced in the larger, longer-lived males.

Reproductive output in Lutreolina crassicaudata is structured around a relatively high fecundity for a marsupial of its size. Females produce litters ranging from 7 to 11 pups per reproductive event [N_R_i = 7 to 11 pups per reproductive event], and they can complete up to 2 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 2 litters per year]. This annual reproductive schedule is supported by the species' use of a thermally stable pouch environment regulated at 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C], which buffers developing young against environmental temperature fluctuations. The combination of moderate litter size with a biannual breeding frequency yields a substantial maximum daily reproductive rate, allowing females to offset the relatively high mortality rates observed in juvenile opossums during their first year. This life-history strategy, characterized by repeated small litters across a single breeding season, is typical of many small to medium-sized didelphids and stands in contrast to the single, large litters produced by some larger marsupials. The capacity for a second annual litter is likely contingent on adequate food availability and the female's ability to regain body condition after weaning the first cohort of offspring.

Pubertal development and the onset of reproductive capability are key transitions in the life cycle of this species. Females attain sexual maturity at 183 days after birth [tp = 183 days after birth] under the standard thermoregulatory conditions of 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C], meaning they become reproductively active within their first calendar year. This relatively early age at puberty, compared with larger didelphids, enables females to contribute to the breeding population soon after reaching adult body size. The timing of first ovulation is tightly linked to both body condition and photoperiod cues, with peak breeding activity often coinciding with seasonal flooding that increases prey availability in riparian zones. The attainment of puberty at approximately six months of age allows young females born early in the breeding season to potentially participate in the second annual litter window later that same year. This early reproductive onset is a key component of the species' relatively fast life-history pace, enabling rapid population turnover in dynamic floodplain environments. Males likely reach puberty at a comparable age, though direct field observations of testicular descent and spermatogenesis remain sparse for this species across its extensive geographic range.

Maximum lifespan in the wild for Lutreolina crassicaudata is estimated at approximately 2.9 years [am = approximately 2.9 years] when averaged across individuals maintaining a body temperature of 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, common among small marsupials, contrasts with the considerably longer documented longevity of larger didelphids such as the Virginia opossum. The rapid life-history schedule — early puberty, multiple annual litters, and modest maximum longevity — fits a pattern of high reproductive turnover that is well suited to unstable wetland habitats. Seasonal flooding, predation from large aquatic birds and carnivorous mammals, and resource fluctuations all likely contribute to the high extrinsic mortality that constrains this species' lifespan. In captivity, individuals may survive somewhat longer, with isolated anecdotal reports of animals exceeding four years, though these outliers are not representative of wild populations. The physiological mechanisms underlying senescence in this species remain poorly characterized, though field data indicate that both reproductive output and body condition decline markedly after the second year of life. This compressed lifespan, combined with a high annual reproductive investment, defines the species' position along the fast end of the marsupial life-history continuum.
